title: Prefetch memory amplification SLO incident — annotated diary & runbook draft
content:
Summary:
We observed a multi-hour SLO degradation on hosted inference caused by unbounded memory growth originating from the prefetch subsystem populating the KV cache. Symptoms looked like a slow memory amplification (not instant OOM) that then triggered eviction cascades and intermittent request deadlocks when evictions and batch prefetching collided. This doc is an annotated incident diary + early runbook draft to help on-call respond faster and prevent recurrence.

Scope and impact:
- Affected surface: hosted API (text generation routes using the continuous-prefetch optimization).
- Customer impact: increased latencies (p50 -> p95 regression), a handful of internal customers observed timeouts and degraded throughput during the window. No customer data loss.
- Hosts impacted: a subset of GPU-backed serving nodes running prefetch-enabled model variants in eu-west-1 and us-central1.

Detection timeline (annotated):
- 2024-10-21 01:14 UTC — Alert: memory-pressure-new-hosts (p95 memory > 85% for 5m) fired. Alert noise low priority initially.
- 01:18 UTC — SRE on-call (Jonah) triaged; saw rising host mem and concurrent increase in kv_cache_inserts_total.
- 01:25 UTC — Latency alert p95>latency-slo for generation-route-3. SRE suspects cache thrash; check KV cache eviction and insert metrics.
- 01:33 UTC — Quick mitigation: disabled prefetch globally on the affected model variant (feature flag). Memory growth slowed but still trending high on some hosts.
- 01:42 UTC — Observed repeated eviction storms (~10-15k evictions/min/node) and occasional deadlock traces in request tracer indicating request threads waiting on eviction locks.
- 02:05 UTC — Temporary scale-up of capacity (added 4 nodes to the cluster) to buy time for investigation and to reduce immediate timeouts.
- 03:10 UTC — Implemented a conservative prefetch throttle by limiting prefetch concurrency per instance (runtime config). Memory trend stabilized over next 2 hours.

Initial hypotheses considered (and why we rejected/accepted):
- Hypothesis A: Cache leak from eviction metadata structures. Rejected: heap profiles showed proportional growth in cache entries rather than leak in metadata objects.
- Hypothesis B: Prefetch fanout amplification: each request's prefetch logic aggressively spawned N asynchronous prefetch jobs, and concurrent batching + prefetch retries caused insert storm. Accepted: metric correlations and request traces supported this.
- Hypothesis C: Continuous batching interaction: warm-up batches caused repeated cache fills for prefixes not yet seen in steady-state. Plausible and likely contributing factor.

Root cause (current working hypothesis):
A recent change to prefetch policy increased the per-request candidate set (aiming to reduce tail latency by warming common cache prefixes). Under normal low concurrency this was harmless, but when throughput briefly spiked the per-request candidates multiplied across concurrent batches and async fanouts. Prefetch was inserting large numbers of distinct KV items without accounting for collision amortization or an upper bound per-request. This created memory amplification: insert rate >> eviction ability, leading to high resident memory, eviction storms, and occasional lock contention on cache structures resulting in deadlocks for request threads waiting for eviction lock.

Why this is different from a simple OOM:
- Growth was gradual and tied to request pattern (not a single runaway allocation).
- Eviction logic still worked but couldn't keep up because insert fanout outran eviction throughput and caused lock contention.
- Deadlocks were secondary: eviction and prefetch attempted to update shared indexes under heavy contention.

Immediate mitigations performed (commands paraphrased):
1) Feature flag flip: set PREFETCH_ENABLED=false for the affected model variant group (rolled back to stable config).
   - Effect: insert rate fell by ~70% within 5 minutes.
2) Throttle prefetch concurrency: set PREFETCH_MAX_CONCURRENCY=2 on nodes where prefetch remained on for testing.
   - Effect: prevented amplification while preserving some warm cache benefits for low-QPS routes.
3) Increase cluster capacity by +4 nodes and trigger controlled rolling restart of the worst offenders to reclaim fragmented memory.
   - Effect: buy time for code fix; reduced tail timeouts.
4) Emergency patch: introduce a per-request prefetch cap (max_inserts_per_request=128) in the runtime config as a rapid deploy (works as a short-term guardrail).

Reproduction recipe (dev cluster):
- Use a traffic replayer with synthetic QPS matching production warm spikes; enable continuous batching with small batch sizes (16-32) and prefetch set to the new candidate set size.
- Observe kv_cache_inserts_total, kv_cache_evictions_total, host_resident_memory_bytes.
- Increase concurrent clients to ~200 to reproduce insert amplification in 15–30 minutes.
- Attach heap profile and contention traces to confirm insertion-heavy growth and eviction lock contention.

Observability gaps discovered:
- No metric that directly measures 'inserts_per_request' (we had kv_cache_inserts_total but not correlated to request counts).
- Eviction latency histogram was coarse and not instrumented to tag by request vs background eviction.
- Lock contention traces were hard to correlate to specific cache operations in traces.

Runbook draft for on-call (quick start):
- Detection triggers: two of the following for >5m:
  - host_resident_memory_bytes_p95 > 80%
  - kv_cache_inserts_total rate > baseline * 4
  - eviction_rate > inserts_rate (sustained) AND p95 latency degradation
- Immediate steps (order matters):
  1) Set PREFETCH_ENABLED=false for model-variant if present (feature flag).
  2) Reduce PREFETCH_MAX_CONCURRENCY to 1 on affected nodes.
  3) If memory continues to climb, set max_inserts_per_request=64 and observe for 10m.
  4) If deadlocks observed (threads stuck on eviction lock): collect thread dump, heap profile and escalate to eng-serving-runtime.
  5) If SLOs remain violated after config mitigations, scale up cluster by +25% as temporary capacity relief and start rolling restarts of top memory hosts.
- Postmortem data to collect during incident:
  - per-request prefetch candidate counts (add instrumentation if missing),
  - per-node inserts/sec and evictions/sec broken down by model variant,
  - heap profiles every 10 minutes during incident window,
  - request traces that include prefetch decision logs.

Short-term engineering mitigations (next 2 weeks):
- Add per-request budget enforcement in prefetch code (hard cap and slow-start behavior). Owner: Marta Liu. Due: 2024-11-08.
- Add 'inserts_per_request' metric and tag insert events with request id for short windows. Owner: Evan Patel. Due: 2024-11-05.
- Improve eviction algorithm to be less lock-heavy (shard indices and background flush). Owner: Serving Runtime team (PR link in artifacts). Due: 2024-11-22.

Monitoring and alerting changes recommended:
- New alert: prefetched_inserts_per_request_p95 > 200 for 5m.
- New dashboard: cache health panel combining inserts/sec, evictions/sec, eviction-latency-histogram, host-resident-memory, and prefetch_concurrency.
- Add trace-span annotation for prefetch insertion operations so contention shows up in distributed traces.

Longer-term design changes (Q1 planning):
- Move prefetch candidate selection to a sampling-based heuristic (probabilistic warms) rather than deterministic fanout.
- Adaptive prefetch: reduce candidate size under increasing insert rates or if eviction pressure detected.
- Formalize cache insertion budgets per-route with enforcement at runtime.

Post-incident notes and open action items:
- [A-101] Add per-request inserts metric (Evan) — in progress — due 2024-11-05.
- [A-102] Patch runtime to enforce per-request prefetch caps (Marta) — in progress — due 2024-11-08.
- [A-103] Shard KV index and reduce eviction lock contention (Serving Runtime) — planned — PR referenced in linked_artifacts.
- [A-104] Update runbook and run tabletop in next SRE ops meeting (Aisha) — todo — due 2024-11-15.

Lessons learned (operational):
- Any optimization that multiplies per-request work must be bounded by a budget; unbounded fanout interacts poorly with batching and concurrency.
- Alerts that consider ratios (inserts vs evictions) are more actionable than absolute memory thresholds alone.
- Small config knobs (prefetch concurrency, per-request cap) saved the day — prioritize having these as fast rollback knobs behind feature flags.

Appendix: commands and artifacts collected during the incident (paraphrased):
- Toggle flag: infractl feature-toggle set PREFETCH_ENABLED false --scope model-variant:abc
- Throttle: runtime-config set PREFETCH_MAX_CONCURRENCY=1 --host-group serving-eu-west
- Emergency cap: runtime-config set PREFETCH_MAX_INSERTS_PER_REQUEST=128 --global
- Heap/profile artifacts: s3://redwood-internal-incidents/prefetch-2024-10-21/profiles/*
- Thread dump samples: attached in linked_artifacts Confluence page.

Notes for reviewers:
- This is a working doc. The aim is to capture what happened, provide a minimal actionable runbook for next incidents, and list immediate engineering actions. Please comment inline or add sprint tasks for the long-term mitigations.
